source.title: Harmonics of Learning: Universal Fourier Features Emerge in Invariant Networks
source.authors: Giovanni Luca Marchetti; Christopher Hillar; Danica Kragic; S. Sanborn

record.tranche_reason: The paper proves a conditional result about the emergence of Fourier features in invariant networks, using algebraic theorems rather than measuring representational similarity across models.
record.gate_note: The paper's theoretical results bear on V5 under stated invariance and weight assumptions. Its empirical experiments evaluate group-table recovery, not recurrence or alignment of representations across models, so those results are not recorded as claim rows. Statements about convergence and features in prior work are cited background, not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The paper proves that any parametric model of a stated class that is invariant to a finite group must have first-layer weights equal to that group's harmonics, up to a linear transformation. This is a theoretical argument that the same features recur across such models (V5). It does not empirically compare features across independently trained models.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors prove that certain invariant models' weights relate closely to the group Fourier transform, and that group structure can be recovered even from approximately invariant models. They frame this as a first step toward explaining universal features. They note several limits: complex-valued weights, unclear coverage beyond models with unitary symmetries (e.g. attention), and localized wavelets/Gabors not being covered.
record.recipe_differences: The paper gives an algebraic theory of Fourier-feature emergence in invariant networks; it does not apply the original studies' empirical cross-model representation-similarity procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The theorem's result depends on its stated assumptions: unitary symmetries and surjective weight components for Theorem 10, with an additional orthogonality condition for the full Fourier-transform conclusion in Corollary 11.
record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, volume 247; 37th Annual Conference on Learning Theory (2024)
record.problems: The theoretical conclusions apply only under specific invariance and parametrization assumptions, and the paper notes that complex-valued weights are non-canonical and that coverage of other primitives is unclear. The empirical section demonstrates group recovery for a limited set of groups; it does not compare representations across models or test the scale-and-capability claim.
record.rows_left_out: The empirical group-recovery results, including the noisy-data table-accuracy plots in Figures 2–3, were left out because their outcome is multiplication-table recovery rather than cross-model feature recurrence or representational alignment. The paper's cited empirical observations are not its own results.

untested.parts: No scaling or capability sweep, and no comparison across architectures, objectives or data.
No vision-language or paired image-caption models.
No direct comparison of features across seeds. The 20-run group-recovery experiment only indirectly implies that each run learns harmonics.
No mapping, stitching or relative-representation experiments.

No empirical feature matching across trained models. The theory covers only complex-weight models with unitary symmetries (spectral networks, single neurons, the first layer of deep nets). It does not cover real-valued weights, attention, or localized wavelet/Gabor features.
No variation of similarity measures or inputs.
No measurement of plateau or of the causes of alignment.

missing.what: Group multiplication table recovered correctly from trained Power-Spectral Network weights across 20 training runs up to a noise threshold. This indirectly implies that runs from different initializations converge to the same harmonic weights. It is a recovery metric, not a feature-similarity measure.

record.verdict_notes: This is a COLT theory paper. The V5 verdict rests on conditional theorems. The scope limits are untested parts, not limits_scope evidence. Statements about universality in the introduction (Gabor filters, grid cells, Li et al. 2015) are cited background, not this study's results.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep over model size or capability, and no comparison of independently trained models with different architectures, objectives, or data.
No vision-language models or paired image-caption representations.
Training runs are not compared for shared features or subspaces across initializations.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired alignment experiment.

The theoretical result is conditional on finite-group invariance and specified properties of the parametrization; the paper does not empirically compare interpretable features or circuits across independently trained models.
No comparison of similarity measures, their settings, or in-distribution versus out-of-distribution representation alignment.
No test of whether alignment plateaus or whether shared training data or objectives explain it.

rows.subject: φ : W → H (parametric function satisfying Theorem 10's assumptions)
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 10 proves a form for the weights of a group-invariant parametrization with unitary symmetries and surjective weight components.

conditions.value: φ(g · W) = φ(W) for all g ∈ G
Wi is surjective for every i

rows.measure: Theoretical weight form: for each i, Wi(g) = Wi′ ρi(g)†, where ρi is an irreducible unitary representation of G.
rows.value: Theorem 10 states that such Wi′ and ρi exist for every i.
rows.note: A conditional mathematical result; it does not report an empirical comparison between different models.
rows.check: Link and state are acceptable. The recurring feature holds only up to a per-unit linear factor Wi′, so models are shown to share harmonics, not identical weights. This is a proof, not a measurement.

rows.subject: φ : W → H (parametric function satisfying Corollary 11's assumptions)
rows.operation_detail: Corollary 11 derives the Fourier-transform form when the invariant parametrization's weights are unitary up to a multiplicative constant.

conditions.value: φ(g · W) = φ(W) for all g ∈ G

rows.measure: Theoretical correspondence of weights to the group Fourier transform.
rows.value: Corollary 11 states that W is the Fourier transform up to composing each component Wi with an operator of Frobenius norm 1.
rows.note: The result concerns the stated invariant-function class and orthogonality condition; it is not an empirical cross-model feature comparison.
rows.check: Link and state are acceptable. Under orthonormality, W equals the group Fourier transform only up to a Frobenius-norm-1 operator on each component. Cross-model identity therefore holds up to that ambiguity.

relationships.condition: Finite-group-invariant models with unitary symmetries and surjective weight components (Theorem 10); full Fourier transform under the orthonormality condition (Corollary 11)
relationships.reason: Theorems prove that every such invariant model's weights are group harmonics up to a linear factor, so the same features must recur (r1, r2). The support is theoretical, not an empirical cross-model test.
relationships.display_finding: The proofs establish weights as group harmonics up to a linear factor, yielding the full Fourier transform under the additional orthonormality condition.
